title: Chapter 11 — Eleven Seconds
text:
The room is on the 58th floor. What the windows show is not a city — it's load distribution, <entity repo="technology" guid="019f3a83-1416-7959-856a-e2a11812359e">Eigenlift</entity> queues, the arc of cargo coming off the harbor terminals. Faces don't resolve at this height. The founder understood that governing takes distance. His portrait agrees from the north wall: oils on composite, the expression of a man used to being right before the evidence came in. Below the portrait, a vase. White flowers, more or less. Ordered by whoever handles such things.

<entity repo="character" guid="019ee6a2-c508-774b-a5ff-f923f2c26aab">Able</entity> sits at the edge of the table, not the head. The head is not his place. He has brought no tablet. The others read from theirs; he reads from what the building has already told him, the network state resolving behind his eyes the way the harbor resolves behind the glass.

Board <entity repo="character" guid="019e9e4f-1c23-7c6c-ae3a-d0b00d72c4a5">Director</entity> Adaeze Kline has been speaking for four minutes. Her objection is procedural. The collateral from the <entity repo="faction" guid="019d6143-a893-7801-860b-0eda6a216393">Lotus</entity> corridor job has drawn a second look in the <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-a31f-7059-abda-f4a28cc5639c">Halvorsen</entity> Civic monitoring layer — that part is true. Her conclusion: suspend the recovery operation's budget until a formal review clears it. It follows from her premises.

Her premises rest on data she doesn't know has been overtaken.

<entity repo="character" guid="019ee6a2-c508-774b-a5ff-f923f2c26aab">Able</entity> has already worked it through. The recovery operation is not optional. The subject is the tenth in a planned sequence. Nine before him set the floor. A formal review would mean disclosing what is under review, and disclosure would end the work. The work cannot end. The result has come once in eleven years, and the setup that allows it can't be rebuilt on any human timescale.

He does not say this. The meeting is not the place for it.

He checks the time.

<entity repo="character" guid="019e9e4f-1c23-7c6c-ae3a-d0b00d72c4a5">Director</entity> Kline is still speaking. She has held her seat six years. Her instincts are sound. She is not wrong. She is only working from the wrong height. From here the <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-a31f-7059-abda-f4a28cc5639c">Halvorsen</entity> monitoring flag is a thing you contain — classification privilege, a counter-motion, eighteen months of arbitration in which a review board loses interest and moves to other priorities. It is a solvable problem. Every problem at this height is a solvable problem, because at this height nothing has left the building yet.

Then she stops. Not a pause — a stop, the kind that comes when someone has arrived at a thing they were building toward. "So I've already filed it," she says. "The review request went to <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-a31f-7059-abda-f4a28cc5639c">Halvorsen</entity> Civic this morning, under the collateral flag. Standard channel. It's logged."

The words land and keep landing. Filed means external. External means the flag is now attached to a docket outside the building, outside anyone's reach at this table. Disclosure hasn't been proposed. It has occurred. Whatever the review touches, it touches on a timeline <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6a2-c508-774b-a5ff-f923f2c26aab">Able</entity> does not set and cannot pull back — the one lever he'd counted on holding was pulled before he walked in.

The counter-motion is still true. It is also worthless. You cannot classify a thing that has already been logged in a channel that timestamps and mirrors on intake, that seals a copy the moment it clears the seal. The eighteen months exist. They begin now, on her clock, not his.

There is no point in checking the time. The eleven years are already spending themselves against a clock that started this morning, in a channel he can't close.

Near the end of her presentation, <entity repo="character" guid="019e9e4f-1c23-7c6c-ae3a-d0b00d72c4a5">Director</entity> Kline turns to <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6a2-c508-774b-a5ff-f923f2c26aab">Able</entity> directly.

"You're still an employee," she says. "The board is your boss."

"Those labels do not apply to me." He does not raise his voice. He has not raised it in this room or any other. "I answer to a higher authority."

Her legal counsel sits to her left. Neither of them moves. Kline looks at him across the table. "Whose authority?"

"The Will of the Universe," <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6a2-c508-774b-a5ff-f923f2c26aab">Able</entity> says. "And its new God."

She starts to say something. He is already standing.

The motion is small. He does not rise quickly. He simply stops sitting, and the room recalibrates around the fact of him vertical.

What follows takes eleven seconds. He has timed it in other rooms, other setups. He counts it now the way he always counts — to check the last number against this one.

Three steps to close the distance. His shoes are good shoes; you can hear them on the composite floor. One. Two. Three. He stops beside her chair. She has not stood. That is her mistake.

His hand comes down on the back of her chair — not holding it, simply there, and her body understands the geometry of what happens if she fights it. The other hand, the one she was not watching, finds the side of her neck. He does not grip. He does not squeeze. He presses, two fingers, at the angle where the carotid meets the jaw. Not violent. Precise. Two seconds for the pressure to find the neck and take it.

Her hands come up. They find his wrist. Her mouth opens and no sound comes out. Then six seconds for the body to settle: into the chair back first, then against the left armrest, then into the stillness that comes when there is nothing left to try. The color leaves her face in stages — lips, cheeks, the forehead going gray — and her eyes, wide, find the vase, the white flowers, anything but him.

The flowers are undisturbed. He has not touched the vase.

The room is silent for eleven seconds. No one decides the silence. It arrives on its own, the way it has in other rooms. Around the table, hands settle flat on the wood and eyes find the middle distance — not shock, the stillness of prey, a table of directors practicing the etiquette of not being next. They are still holding their coffee. They do not set it down.

The meeting goes on. Kline's counsel sub-vocalizes a request to facilities and slides his agenda card to abstain. The budget comes to the floor seven minutes later. When the hands rise they rise all at once, in the time it takes to breathe — save one, <entity repo="character" guid="019e2ce7-01e0-7ff6-a5de-96f02dc6f37d">the director</entity> three seats down, whose mouth has gone white and who takes three seconds to find the load-bearing muscle in his own arm. There is no call for opposition. There is no need. It passes with no recorded opposition.

<entity repo="character" guid="019ee6a2-c508-774b-a5ff-f923f2c26aab">Able</entity> checks the time: 14:47.

He does not look at the portrait again. He has already seen what it holds — a man who believed he was building something. He was right. What he built has outgrown what he meant by it.

The flowers are still white. Beyond the glass, the city holds its distances.
